items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: We had tunes from Basie’s book

ctx.x: Tell us about the first time you heard bebop. And do you remember what your reaction was?

Yeah I remember the first time I heard it. It wasn’t on — was it on records or not? I think it was probably the same time — I was in high school, or I had just graduated from high school I think, or maybe during my last year of high school. I really was getting into it. And so there was a saxophone player who was a good friend of mine who was really a Lester Young fanatic. And then he heard Charlie Parker, you know and he was talking about Charlie Parker. He says, “Oh you’ve got to listen to this.” So I went over…

Harold was a frustrated trumpet player himself. But he was a good musician, he knew about the theory of music. So he would trade bands a set of uniforms if they let him copy like some of the tunes from their book. Like we had tunes from Basie’s book, and remember the Billy Eckstine Big Band? We had some of those tunes. We had a couple of Dizzy’s tunes. We had a lot of Stan Kenton tunes, some Woody Herman things. The book was about that thick with all these things, you know all these charts. And we got all these…

items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Because I tell them stories like Sweets Edison told me once that the Basie Band of the late ‘30s and early ‘40s did not have a book

ctx.x: Um humm. In fact, we try to work more on heads rather than music. Some things we might use say a lead sheet. But if you notice blues bands, they’re very improvisational on the gig. You know you hear them come up with these backgrounds and things, you know like making up just on the spot. And this is what I’m trying to teach them to do and they love that. The first couple of weeks they’re kind of in the dark, then somebody will — as they used to say in the old days — set a riff, and they pick it up like that. And…

And you have to be a sophomore to get into my class. So they are pretty well trained on things like that by the time they get there. It works good. Because I tell them stories like Sweets Edison told me once that the Basie Band of the late ‘30s and early ‘40s did not have a book, they had no written music. And some of those early records you hear are head arrangements. I say are you serious? He says yeah. Somebody in a section will just like pay a riff and I guess their ears are so trained from playing jazz, jazz…
Yeah, in fact I hear stories about guys who used to accidentally lose parts from things that got too difficult.
